analytic.title: Scheduling Techniques to Integrate MPEG-based Multimedia Applications in Hard Real-Time Systems

div.p: In this paper, we propose scheduling techniques to provide efficient run-time support to MPEG-based multimedia applications in the real-time system, where multimedia tasks and hard real-time tasks can coexist simultaneously. The paper describes a server-based mechanism for assigning the CPU resource to two types of tasks. Especially for MPEG video applications, we show how to dynamically control the fraction of the CPU bandwidth allocated to each multimedia task without jeopardizing the schedulability of hard real-time tasks present in the system. Scheduling techniques of this mechanism are capable o f minimizing the mean tardiness of multimedia tasks while satisfying the timing consbaints of hard real-time tasks.

div.head: Introduction
div.p: Real-time control applications can benefit significantly fiom the incorporation of multimedia information into the control environment[l, 21. Hard real-time applications like automated manufacturing and attack helicopters are being designed to take advantage of audio and video information [3]. This multimedia information is less critical than hard real-time control information but needs real-time support because o f the sensitivity to delay and jitter tolerance. Support for processing this information must, on the other hand, co-exist with that for the hard real-time control information [4]. In hard real-time systems for handling multimedia applications, two types of tasks can coexist simultaneously: hard real-time tasks and multimedia tasks modeled as soft real-time tasks. Accommodating multimedia soft and traditional hard real-time applications that have interaction requirements is a challenging research issue.

In recent years, there has been an abundance of research in the area of scheduling algorithms [2][3][4][5][6][7]. In general, they are based on a conventional real-time scheduler such as EDF(Earliest Deadline First) or RM(Rate Monotonic). In [5, 61, a scheduling methodology is proposed to reserve a fraction of the processor bandwidth to each task. To efficiently handle the problem of task overloads, each task is scheduled by a dedicated server, which does not require the knowledge of the WCET(Worst Case Execution Time) and assigns a suitable deadline to the served task whenever the reserved time is consumed. Periodic tasks for MPEG streams do not, however, have special treatment in this scheduling method.

In this paper, we discuss how to provide efficient run-time support to MPEG-based multimedia applications in a realtime system, where two types of tasks interact via shared use of the CPU. Hard real-time tasks are guaranteed based on worst case execution times, whereas multimedia soft real-time tasks are served based on mean parameters [5]. In practice, treating MPEG-based multimedia tasks as hard real-time tasks is not appropriate, firstly because an underestimation of the WCET would compromise the guarantee done on the other tasks. Secondly, it would be very inefficient, since hying to guarantee a task with a WCET much greater than its mean execution time would cause a waste of the CPU resource.

In order to integrate multimedia and hard real-time tasks in the same system, we propose a multimedia server that partitions its CPU bandwidth between two types of tasks. This server fixes the maximum time that all hard real-time use in its period and the maximum time that multimedia tasks use in the same period. Within the corresponding maximum time a fraction of the CPU bandwidth is reserved to each hard real-time task and multimedia task, respectively. Every hard real-time task based on the WCET can get its requested hction of time in the server because it requires more deterministic guarantee. In practice, due to the high variability in multimedia stream processing, it is not desirable to schedule multimedia tasks within the server in the way hard real-time tasks are processed. For flexibility in execution of multimedia tasks, we show how to effectively control the Gaction of the CPU bandwidth allocated to each task. The primary goal of our research is 0-7803-8185-8/03/$17.00 0 2003 IEEE to minimize the mean tardiness that multimedia tasks execute after their deadlines while guaranteeing all the hard real-time tasks within given deadlines.

div.head: Scheduling schemes 2.1 Bandwidth allocation scheme
div.p: In this paper, we integrate MPEG-based multimedia and hard real-time tasks using a multimedia server. div.head: Priority-based scheduling
div.p: A multimedia task may require more than or less than the reserved bandwidth according to the size of the frame [9]. In order to minimize the tardiness that a multimedia task executes after its deadline, the proposed server allows it to share the available CPU bandwidth allocated to other multimedia tasks according to the priority. We assume that each fiame within a GoP is assigned a single task for decoding. We define three task classes that represent the different importance of tasks in a video system. I-fiame decoding tasks are assigned to Class-I, whereas P -h e decoding tasks are inserted into the queue of Class-2 with lower priority than Class-I. Class-3 with the lowest priority consists of B-fiame decoding tasks.

In fact, it is not possible to decode a B-6ame without having decoded the respective Ior P-6ame fust[lO]. This priority-based scheduling policy also gives decoding tasks for I-fiames higher priority over those for P-6ames. Each task class is assigned a working queue that sorts all executable tasks in order of priority, serving the highest priority fmt. Within tasks with the same priority the task with the earliest deadline is scheduled fmt. Multimedia tasks in each class are non-preemptive. Thus, a multimedia task in each class is not preempted by other multimedia task in this paper.

div.head: Preemption policy
div.p: It is assumed that hard real-time tasks have higher priority than multimedia tasks in this paper. Hard real-time tasks are assigned to top priority, Class-0. We adopt a policy of preemption in order to give a preference to hard real-time tasks with the highest priority. With the help of preemption policy, the timing constraint of the hard real-time task is never sacrificed in this paper.

div.head: Experimental results
div.p: Experiments have been conducted to test the performance of the proposed multimedia server. In this section we compare our flexible reservation scheme(FRS) with other constant reservation scheme(CRS). In CRS, every multimedia task must get its fraction of the CPU bandwidth in the server. When a multimedia task needs more than its reserved bandwidth in CRS, it is queued until the next server instance arrives in the system. Meanwhile, such multimedia task can be scheduled in the same server instance by sharing the available CPU bandwidth of other tasks in FRS. All simulations presented in this section have been conducted on a hybrid task set consisting of TI, T2, T3 and Ta in the above example described in Figure 2. The actual execution times of the multimedia tasks are randomly generated using a uniform distribution between the minimum decoding time and the maximum decoding time of each kame in Table 1. For simplicity, it is assumed that T2 and T4 have the same GoP pattern with N= 15 and 3.

In the first experiment, we compare the mean tardiness experienced by multimedia tasks, T2 and T4, when they are served by a FRS and a CRS. In the simulation, all bard realtime tasks meet their deadlines using the budget in the server. Therefore, all the simulation results shown in this section are obtained fiom MPEG-based multimedia tasks, T2 and T4. The simulation results are illustrated in Figure 3, which shows that the performance of the CRS is worse than the one achieved by the FRS. In Figure 3, the FRS and the CRS curves can be better distinguished, so we can see that the tardiness experienced by multimedia tasks under the CRS is higher than that experienced using the FRS. This is because the FRS is more efficient to handle the variable decoding times of each frame than the CRS. In the second experiment we represented the number of decoded frames as a function of time for T2 and T4. In fact, the CRS can cause an underutilization of the processor when scheduling multimedia tasks. As shown in Table 2, the FRS decodes more frames than the CRS during the same amount of time by utilizing the CPU bandwidth effectively. This result was expected for the reasons explained above. In Table 2, the unit of time is second.

div.head: Conclusion
div.p: We presented scheduling algorithms of the multimedia server that enables guaranteed execution of traditional hard real-time tasks and allows to nicely integrate MPEG-based multimedia tasks with them. The proposed server can adjust effectively a fraction of the CPU time to multimedia tasks according to the priority. For flexibility in execution of multimedia tasks, we use a priority-based scheduling policy that gives I-frame decoding tasks higher priority over Pframe decoding tasks and assigns the decoding task for Pframe higher priority than that for B-li'ame. This server also gives a preferential treatment to hard real-time tasks with the highest priority. With the help of the preemption policy, the server can always satisfy the timimg constraints of hard real-time tasks. The objective of this server is to minimize the mean tardiness of multimedia tasks, without jeopardizing the schedulability of the hard real-time tasks.

We showed through simulations that the tardiness experienced by multimedia tasks under the proposed FRS is much smaller than that experienced by using the CRS. As can be seen from experiment results, the FRS performs better than the CRS. The proposed adaptive scheduling techniques can be applied to multimedia systems for MPEG video streams in order to improve the performance. These scheduling techniques are also expected to support an adaptive QoS degradation of multimedia sessions during system overload.
